rows.verified: Paper and tissue manufacture and processing can expose workers to paper or tissue dust that affects the respiratory system.
COSHH requires employers to protect workers from harmful exposure to paper and tissue dust.
Paper dust can fall within COSHH at or above 10 mg/m3 inhalable dust or 4 mg/m3 respirable dust as an eight-hour time-weighted average.
Cellulose in tissue dust has workplace exposure limits of 10 mg/m3 inhalable and 4 mg/m3 respirable dust.
Contact with moving machinery is a major cause of injury in paper and corrugated-board operations.
After machinery modification, adequate guarding must be replaced before the machine is returned to use.
Common manual-handling tasks include moving paper, bales and board stacks, removing broke and handling machine parts.
Regular access at height to machinery requires properly constructed access platforms, handrails or other effective fall controls.
Paper-industry risk depends on dust concentration, machine type, web speed, intervention frequency, bale weight, access design and control maintenance.
Paper evidence is process-, machine-, dust-, task- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury or respiratory-risk probability.
Textile employers must protect employees and other people who may be affected, including customers, neighbours and members of the public.
Textile safety topics include fire, dust, chemicals, dyes, knives, machinery and bale handling.
Some reactive dyes are respiratory sensitisers that can cause occupational asthma, and some dyes can sensitise skin.
Sodium hydrosulphite can react violently if added incorrectly and must not contact residual oxidising agents.
Using liquid, granular, dust-suppressed or other low-dusting dye forms can reduce exposure.
Dispensing powdered or granular reactive dyes should be carried out under local exhaust ventilation.
Cotton and wool process dust can contribute to explosion risk, respiratory irritation, asthma or byssinosis; cleaning should use vacuum methods rather than brooms or compressed air.
Health surveillance can identify early ill health and control failure but does not replace elimination or effective risk control.
Textile risk depends on fibre, dye chemistry, dustiness, process temperature, machinery, extraction, cleaning and individual sensitisation.
Textile evidence is fibre-, chemical-, process-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness or accident probability.
